rounds.what: The branch's diff changed since round 1 — three code commits answering the review's twelve threads, then a forward merge of main@origin — so this is a full round over the changed surface, not a fingerprint re-check. The two correctness fixes the architect named were each driven by reproducing the defect they fix, and the change's central claim about the API server was moved off a simulation onto a real Kubernetes API server.

implementerProof.how: Round 2: I re-ran both of this round's proofs that name a production-like surface at my own head build (provision with the branch merged and deleted; `legion start --check-config` on a staged example), and I checked its three negative controls by performing the reverts myself in an out-of-tree copy of the module rather than taking them on trust — each failed exactly as its handoff says, and each test passes again when restored. The one claim of its proof 2 that rested on a simulation (a schema walker that reproduces the API server's pruning) I drove on a real Kubernetes API server instead, which both confirmed its conclusion and corrected one word of it (see proof 2 below). Its fingerprint proof across the forward merge I did not recompute, because the diff is not the one my round 1 verified: new code lands in it, so a fingerprint comparison would answer a question nobody is asking; I tested the changed surface instead. Round 1: I re-ran both of that round's production-like proofs independently and read all 17 hits of its deletion grep.

proof.criterion: The cutover's two correctness fixes: the replacement Sandbox carries the `legion.dev/displaced-pod` name its predecessor was given, and an init container the daemon's own delete killed is not a failed init.
proof.surface: The package's own rig — the real `relaunch`, `verdict` and `Probe` paths against an httptest API server — driven as a defect reproduction rather than as a suite: the fix reverted in an out-of-tree copy of the module, the failure observed, the fix restored, the test green again. This is the same shape as round 1's migration-0051 proof: the hazard reproduced, then shown cured.
proof.command: In /tmp/mods/daemon (a copy of packages/daemon at this head): revert `ended.initFailed = initExit != nil && pod.DeletionTimestamp == nil` to `initExit != nil` and run `go test ./internal/runtime/sandbox -run 'TestTheMappingRowByRowInPrecedence|TestALaunchReplacesTheIssueSandboxOfTheSupersededDiskShape'`; restore; then drop the `displacedAnnotation` copy from `replaceSupersededSandbox` and run the second test; restore and re-run both
proof.observed: Without the failed-init fix: `TestTheMappingRowByRowInPrecedence/5 an init container the daemon's own delete killed is no failed init` fails with `initFailed = true, want false` and `Displaced = false, want true`, on a pod whose init container terminated `Error, exit code 137` — the kubelet's SIGKILL of the init container the daemon itself was deleting. That is the cutover defect in the open: every role of such a pod would be read as plain Gone and charged a death, and the architect's point that this lands on the cutover launch of every running issue is what makes it matter. Without the annotation carry: `TestALaunchReplacesTheIssueSandboxOfTheSupersededDiskShape` fails with `the Sandbox this launch created names "" as the pod the daemon replaced, want uid-pod-old`. Both pass at this head.
proof.negativeControl: A mutation the implementer did not run: inverting the new guard to `pod.DeletionTimestamp != nil`, so a genuinely failed init in a live pod would read as not failed and a pod whose init keeps failing would be resumed into rather than replaced. Four tests catch it, among them `TestRestartingInitFailureIsGoneForEveryRole`, `TestColdInitFailureReachesSupervisionWithoutWaitingForLauncher` and the row `5 the same init container terminating non-zero in a pod nothing is deleting is a failed init` — so the guard is pinned in both directions, not only in the one the fix moved. (Three further failures in that run — `TestCheckPodRefusesWhatCollidesWithLegionsOwn`, `TestCheckPodHoldsDispatchPublicURLToTheAgentsRule`, `TestTheReclaimParagraphNamesEveryDirectoryTheRendererPutsOnTheIssueVolume` — are an artefact of my out-of-tree copy: each reads a repository file by a relative path that does not exist beside the copy, and each fails the same way with no mutation applied. Checked, not assumed.)

proof.criterion: 1. The disk carries no labels and the Sandbox owns no claim template — and the cutover's delete-and-create is the only way out of the old shape.
proof.surface: A **real Kubernetes API server, v1.37** (etcd and kube-apiserver from the envtest assets, run in this pod under its own token auth) with **the pinned production Agent Sandbox CRD** (`internal/runtime/sandbox/testdata/sandboxes.agents.x-k8s.io.yaml`) applied to it, and the daemon's own rendered Sandbox (`testdata/golden/worker.json`) submitted to it. This replaces a simulation with the thing simulated: until now the pruning claim rested on a schema walker that reproduces the API server's behaviour.
proof.command: `kubectl apply -f testdata/sandboxes.agents.x-k8s.io.yaml`; `kubectl create -f testdata/golden/worker.json`; read back `.spec.podTemplate.spec.volumes[0]` and `.spec.volumeClaimTemplates`; POST the same object with labels on the ephemeral claim template's metadata, once through kubectl and once through a client that sets no `fieldValidation` (as the daemon's dynamic client does); `kubectl patch --type=merge` adding `spec.volumeClaimTemplates`; then the cutover sequence — create an old-shape Sandbox owning the `issue` template, send the exact merge patch `suspendDisplacing` sends, delete, and create the new shape carrying the annotation
proof.observed: The daemon's rendered Sandbox is accepted unchanged: the pod's one disk comes back as `ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplate` with `metadata: {}`, ReadWriteOnce, the configured class and size, and `.spec.volumeClaimTemplates` is absent. A claim template carrying labels is **pruned**: through a client that sets no field validation the create returns **201** with the stored metadata `{}` — and a `warning: 299 - unknown field "spec.podTemplate.spec.volumes[0].ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplate.metadata.labels"` header, so "without a word" (the phrase in `podkind.go`'s comment and in round 1's own write-up, which was mine too) is one word too strong; there is a warning, which the daemon does not surface. Adding `volumeClaimTemplates` to a live Sandbox is refused by the CRD's own rule: `The Sandbox … is invalid: spec: Invalid value: volumeClaimTemplates is immutable` — the premise of `replaceSupersededSandbox` confirmed on a real API server rather than read out of the YAML. The cutover sequence runs end to end: the old shape is accepted, the suspension merge patch returns **200** with `{"legion.dev/displaced-pod": "uid-pod-old"}` and `operatingMode: Suspended` **in the patch's own response** — which is precisely what this round's fix reads, and why `suspendDisplacing` had to return the patched object — and the replacement of the new shape, carrying that annotation and owning no claim template, is accepted.
proof.negativeControl: The same labelled object through kubectl, which sets `fieldValidation=Strict`: a hard refusal, `BadRequest … strict decoding error: unknown field "spec.podTemplate.spec.volumes[0].ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplate.metadata.labels"`, and nothing created. So the field is genuinely unknown to the schema under both validation modes, and the difference between pruning and refusal is the client's, not the schema's.

proof.criterion: 2. An issue whose branch has been merged and deleted starts its agents — re-verified at this head, with the dead sessions directory gone.
proof.surface: The real `legion workspace-init provision` binary built from this head, against a real bare remote and a real feed mirror on the issue's own disk.
proof.command: `legion workspace-init provision --issue ACME-1 --repo acme/widgets --default-branch main --root $TMPDIR/p2/root --credential-helper '!true' --feed $TMPDIR/p2/feed` with `refs/heads/legion/ACME-1` deleted from the feed, then `ls -a` of the root
proof.observed: Exit 0, `workspace-init: … on legion/ACME-1 from main`, the workspace holding `a.txt` alone on an empty commit over `main`. The root holds `repos` and `workspaces` **and nothing else** — the `<root>/sessions` directory I reported as dead state in round 1 is gone from the real command's output, not only from a test (review thread 4369871423).
proof.negativeControl: The same command with the branch fetched back into the feed put `b.txt` in the workspace — the branch's own commit — so the deleted-branch run read the deletion rather than never looking for a branch.

proof.criterion: 5. A deployment cannot keep sessions as files on a disk that dies with its pod — re-verified at this head, and the runtime's own refusal behind it.
proof.surface: The real `legion start --check-config` CLI against the example with its token files, App PEMs and kubeconfig staged, and the real `sandbox.New` entry point for the defence the review added behind it.
proof.command: `legion start --check-config` on the example and on five variants; then a program calling `sandbox.New` with an otherwise valid `Options` whose `SessionDSNKey` is empty
proof.observed: The example exits 0 (`Config OK: project=WIDGETS`); `pvc`, the key omitted entirely and `Postgres` each exit 1 with the one store message; `postgres` with no `session_dsn_secret` exits 1 naming the key; an empty key exits 1 saying it must not be empty. `sandbox.New` with no key refuses before anything else: `sandbox runtime: no session database URL key: the providers Secret's key holding the postgres:// URL every role's Oh My Pi keeps its session in is required …`, so an `Options` built by hand cannot reach a launch either.
proof.negativeControl: The unmodified example exits 0, so the loader's refusal is the store's and not a broken fixture; and the same `Options` with the key named but an unpinned image gives the image's refusal instead, so the key check is what fired in the first case and not a blanket rejection.

proof.criterion: 1. No disk outlives a pod. The disk a pod is given is created with it and deleted with it, at the size and on the storage used today, and it is found by its name, which is the pod's with `-issue` after it, and by its pod owner, since Kubernetes keeps no labels on a disk of this kind.
proof.surface: A real Kubernetes cluster. The build namespace this worker pod may submit Jobs to admits exactly the volume shape this change renders for an issue pod — a new filesystem generic ephemeral volume of a scratch storage class whose claim template carries no labels or annotations — so I ran a pod declaring the same `spec.volumes[].ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplate` the goldens show, with the namespace's claim counter as the observation Legion's own tests cannot make. The ephemeral volume the goldens render is unchanged this round, so this proof stands at the new head.
proof.command: kubectl apply -f (Job infra-80-disk-cc8c2e: gvisor, one 4-CPU container, one ephemeral 20Gi claim template with empty metadata), then `kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.volumes[0]}'`, `kubectl logs`, the namespace's claim counter polled through the pod's life, and `kubectl delete job`
proof.observed: The claim counter went 0 → 1 while the pod was still Pending, so the claim is created with the pod and not with the container. The pod's own spec carried the template back unchanged. At first mount the disk held `lost+found` alone, 19.5G free of a 20Gi claim, and took a 16 MiB write. The counter stayed at 1 after the pod reached Completed, so the claim's life is the pod object's, not the container's — which is why Legion's suspend, which deletes the pod, is what deletes the disk. After `kubectl delete job`, the pod was gone at the first poll and the counter was back to 0 at the next, about one second later; `kubectl get jobs,pods` then showed nothing of the run.
proof.negativeControl: The same Job with one label on that claim template, submitted server-side with nothing created: refused by the namespace's admission policy naming the rule. Round 2 reached the same conclusion from the pinned CRD on a real API server.
proof.doesNotSettle: That the Agent Sandbox controller hands an ephemeral pod volume through to the pod untouched. The live Stage 4a run against b650d854 answered that question in the affirmative — the claim created by `kube-system:ephemeral-volume-controller` and owned by the pod with `controller: true` — and nothing yet shows the disk going with its pod on a real cluster, which the queued rerun is what settles.

proof.criterion: 6. Nothing is left behind at the cutover — the upgrade half: an issue_suspend row the running release queued must still run after the daemon is upgraded.
proof.surface: A real PostgreSQL 16, brought up as a workload in the cluster and reached by its Service name from this pod, carrying the daemon's own schema and driven by the daemon's own migration runner and its own enqueue path, with the payload bytes produced by `json.Marshal` of `record.IssueSuspend` exactly as the release before this change declares it. Migration 0051 and `record.IssueSuspend` are untouched this round, so this proof stands at the new head.
proof.command: Open the database, migrate it, delete the schema_version row for 51 so it stands where a deployment on the running release stands, enqueue the two rows that release writes, decode each with `record.DecodeOutboxPayload`, then run `store.Migrate` again as the upgrade does and decode again
proof.observed: At schema 50 the head binary refuses the releasing row — `decode outbox row 1: json: unknown field "release"` — the stall the migration exists to prevent, reproduced rather than argued. The upgrade applied exactly 1 migration. Both rows then decode, and every other column of both — attempts 2, next_at, last_error and created_at — is byte-identical before and after, so a row in the middle of its retry backoff keeps it.
proof.negativeControl: The keeping row, written without the key, decoded before the migration and was left untouched by it — the `payload ? 'release'` guard selects the rows that need it and nothing else.

proof.criterion: 5. No code is left that reuses, repairs or inspects a disk from an earlier pod, with the stale git-lock sweep kept for the retry on the same disk.
proof.surface: The tree, plus the one runtime surface where a provision can still meet a non-empty disk — the kubelet restarts a failed init container in the same pod (`RestartPolicy: Always`).
proof.command: The deletion grep re-run, then `provision` again into a root it had already provisioned after planting this issue's own production failure signature in the clone: `refs/jj/keep/badref` naming a commit the clone does not hold
proof.observed: 17 hits, each history, a contract note, a deliberate statement that the thing is gone, or a negative assertion in the live proofs. With the planted bad ref, provision exits 1 in 0.98 s with `fatal: bad object refs/jj/keep/badref` — no repair attempted, no hang, no half-success, which is what leaves the pod replaceable.
proof.negativeControl: With four stale git locks planted instead, the same command removed each by name and exited 0 — the sweep that must stay works, the repair that must be gone is gone.

ciAtCodeHead.note: Read, not re-run; I waited for no lane. These are the pull request's first runs since the review, because a conflicting pull request starts no `on: pull_request` run at all and the head before the forward merge was never judged. Lint, types and every unit and integration suite are CI's, including the daemon packages this pod cannot run and the daemon tests the spec names as acceptance 3's proof. The one `go test` I ran was the defect reproduction above, on a reverted copy outside the tree, not a lane re-run.

notReachedHere: The seven inverted Stage 4a per-check assertions — `suspend`, `cleanup-reaps-the-issue`, `issue-suspend-resume`, `re-adopt`, `secrets-old-uid-and-revocation`, `displaced`, `kill-launcher` — are **unrun, not passing**. The live run against b650d854 died at `root-ready` on the marker path before reaching them; that cause is fixed at this head and a rerun is arranged with the deployment owner. Until it reports, nothing in this pull request shows an issue's disk going with its pod on a real cluster.
Stage 4b has run at no head at all. Its harness no longer asserts behaviour this change replaced, but a harness that compiles is not a harness that has run.
Acceptance 4 — an agent carrying on from the session database into a replacement pod — needs a Legion daemon against a cluster running the Agent Sandbox controller, which no worker pod can reach.

Acceptance 3's three cases (a paused issue, an issue handed to a new tree, an issue whose pod dies mid-turn) are daemon-level orchestration the spec itself names daemon tests as the proof of; they run in CI's Tests lane.
Acceptance 6's cutover and the six named issues — a person's reading of a deployment.
residualRisks: An issue pod's name is stable, so its generic ephemeral claim is always named `<pod>-issue`; a replacement pod created before the predecessor's claim is reaped stays Pending until it is. Measured on a real cluster in round 1: about one second from the pod's deletion to the claim leaving the namespace's quota, against a 120 s boot timeout, with `waitedOut` now printing a Pending pod's events. Accepted as a risk by the architect.

Every pod start depends on the repository cache; a production check's wake up to fourteen days after the merge may find it swept. The provision itself is cheap — 4.8 s and 148 MB for sjawhar/legion from a local feed, against a 30-minute CloneTimeout.
observations: Correction to round 1, mine to make: I wrote that a label on the ephemeral claim template is pruned by the API server "without a word", repeating `podkind.go`'s comment. On a real API server the create returns 201 with the field dropped **and** a `warning: 299` header naming it, which the daemon's dynamic client receives and does not surface. The conclusion — no labels on the disk, so it is found by name and pod owner — is unchanged.

The reviewer's `Look at first` line in the pull request body still names `sandbox.go:255-280` as "the file-session mode the config now refuses is still live in the runtime", which this round deleted; it is the reviewer's line to rewrite at the head it reviews next, not mine.

The body's three unproven claims are stated at their real strength — the seven Stage 4a checks as "unrun, not passing", Stage 4b as never run, and the pass-through as answered by the first run with the disk's deletion still unshown. I checked each against the architect's instruction and found no line overstating them.
